6
The graph shows the variation with time of the acceleration of a car.
acceleration
time
0
0
What must the shaded area under the graph represent?
A
the average velocity of the car
B
the change in velocity of the car
C
the final velocity of the car
D
the initial velocity of the car

hints: Look at the axes of the shaded rectangle: vertical is acceleration in $\text{m s}^{-2}$ and horizontal is time in $\text{s}$.
Connect the axes with the definition $a = (v - u)/t$, so multiplying height by width gives $(\text{m s}^{-2}) \times (\text{s})$.
Ask whether that product gives the total velocity or only how much the velocity has grown, given that the starting velocity is not shown on the graph.
walkthrough: Identify the graph: constant acceleration versus time from $t = 0$, with the shaded area forming a rectangle of height $a$ and width $t$.
State the governing rule: acceleration is rate of change of velocity, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ where $\Delta v = v - u$.
Rearrange to $\Delta v = a \times \Delta t$, which is height multiplied by width and therefore the area under the acceleration-time graph.
Check units: $(\text{m s}^{-2}) \times (\text{s}) = \text{m s}^{-1}$, the unit of velocity change, confirming the interpretation.
Note that initial velocity $u$ is not given and final velocity $v = u + \Delta v$ needs $u$, so the area must be only the change, not the initial, final or average velocity. This is option B

A.explanation: Area has units of velocity, but nothing in the acceleration-time rectangle gives total displacement divided by total time.

B.explanation: Since $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$, then $a \times t = \Delta v$, which is exactly the rectangular area under the acceleration-time graph.

C.explanation: Final velocity equals initial velocity plus change in velocity, so the area alone cannot give it without the starting velocity.

D.explanation: The graph starts at $t = 0$ but the area accumulates after that time, so it cannot represent the velocity already present at the start.
